problem: The halting set is named A_TM. In standard textbooks A_TM means acceptance ({⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w}), while the halting problem is usually called HALT (or K). A student who has memorised A_TM as acceptance will be confused, and may lose marks writing this name in an exam.
fix: Rename it: 'a reduction from the halting problem HALT = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w}', and keep A_TM only if you explicitly say A_TM here means halting.

problem: The example is titled 'Use Rice's theorem', but steps 3–6 do a full reduction from halting instead of applying the theorem. Steps 1–2 already prove FIN undecidable by Rice, so the rest reads like a contradiction of the title and can make students think every Rice application needs a fresh reduction.
fix: Either stop after 'P is nontrivial, so by Rice's theorem FIN is undecidable', or retitle the example 'FIN is undecidable: Rice's theorem and the underlying reduction' and say explicitly that steps 3–6 replay the proof of Rice's theorem, not a new argument.

problem: 'The dashed path is the case ∅ ∉ P' is misleading: the whole diagram is drawn under the assumption ∅ ∉ P, so the dashed edge does not mark that case. The dashed edge is only the branch where M′ loops and accepts ∅, which is outside P precisely because ∅ ∉ P.
fix: 'The dashed branch uses the assumption ∅ ∉ P: there M′ accepts nothing, so L(M′) = ∅ lies outside P. If ∅ ∈ P, the same construction is run on the complement property and the yes/no answers are swapped.'
